3D Chips Push EDA Into New Territory

18

Shares

2

12

3

As AI chips move to stacked, chiplet-based architectures, EDA vendors are reworking mature tools for cross-domain analysis, faster exploration, and agentic AI assistance.

September 24th, 2026 -

By: Liz Allan

Key Takeaways:

EDA tools are helping design 3D-ICs and multi-die systems by co-optimizing across domains and speeding up design exploration.
Customers face several pain points, including vendor interoperability, dynamic floor-planning, IR analysis, and STA analysis.
Agentic AI adds an extra layer on existing tools and serves as the foundation for new startup solutions.

As demand for AI power and performance grows, chip designs increasingly involve 3D stacking, chiplets, and heterogeneous integration within a single package.
In a virtuous cycle, EDA tool vendors are leveraging advanced chips to simulate multi-physics challenges in a single tool instead of running individual solvers. Agentic AI is adding another layer of analysis to enable faster design exploration and automate various tasks. However, a few speed bumps remain due to the rapid progression of chip technology.
One challenge is that HPC/AI chip design must be considered across compute, memory, interconnect, power, and thermal constraints. “Today, nearly every AI accelerator has a process threshold where the hardest problems no longer live inside the chip. They live at the system boundaries,” said Artour Levin, vice president of AI silicon engineering at Microsoft.[1] “A standalone chip is not very beneficial for AI because very few things can be run on a single chip. You really need to look at the system level, and if you look at the history of EDA tools when they started, 30 or 40 years ago, it’s natural that EDA tools were designed to design chips, not a system.”
The chip-to-system threshold is where customers are facing challenges. “The design toolchain grew up around clean abstraction boundaries — cell, block, chip — with physics handled as episodic, domain-by-domain validation at the end,” said Hardik Kabaria, CEO and co-founder of Vinci. “That operating model worked when the hardest problems stayed inside those boundaries. It breaks when heat, stress, and electrical behavior move across the entire physical stack, because the physics insight arrives after the decisions that needed it have already been made. Hardware teams don’t need physics after the design is done changing. They need physics while the design is still moving.”
That requires new approaches, not a faster version of the old workflow. “It’s deterministic, solver-accurate physics that’s continuously available across chip, package, board, and system — treating physics as infrastructure rather than a late-stage checkpoint,” said Kabaria. “In hardware, plausible isn’t enough. Outputs have to be measurable, deterministic, and accurate enough to support real design decisions, which is why solver-grounded results and run-to-run reproducibility matter as much as speed.”
The central question is whether to augment existing EDA tools that have been fine-tuned and proven over many years, or create new tools because AI/HPC chip designs are so different from the monolithic chips of days gone by.
“There are decades of embedded knowledge for good reason, and a lot of long-held beliefs that work in single isolation, but maybe not when you go cross-domain,” said Henry Sheng, executive director of R&D at Synopsys.[2] “This has to be reflected within the tooling itself. How do you manage not to try to boil the ocean? If you try to reinvent everything, you won’t do it. You have to reinvent how you put things together to maintain coherency, so you don’t have different data representations and terminologies for the same thing across domains. Then, how do you bring all that into a cohesive tool?”
Heterogeneity puts more pressure on floor-planning challenges, in particular. “It becomes much harder, and that’s one of the conversations that people are having,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of Keysight EDA. “Can we do the floor planning upfront? Can we make sure we all agree that this is the budget that you get for loss here, and this is the budget I get for signal path, and this is the way we are going to supply power to this complex 3D environment? That conversation starts happening up front, and it leaves very little room for negotiation later.” And while the big money says to use 3D design for AI chips, it can be applicable anywhere, Kamdar added.
Maybe in the future, 3D and heterogeneous design will be out of the box, but that’s not the reality now. “Because the manufacturing and packaging technology is evolving fast, there’s still different solutions out there,” said Michal Siwinski, executive vice president, chief product and marketing officer at Arteris. “You can do it this way. You can do it that way. It’s not yet one size fits all. Because of that, people want some differentiation. But is the technology 80% there? Is it 90% there, where anybody who actually wants to do it can do it? Yeah, I think so.”
Specific customer challenges
Customers designing 3D-ICs and multi-die assemblies for AI/HPC chips are using existing EDA tools, but they want improvements in some areas.
One challenge is interoperability across established vendors and startups. “If you want to put out compelling products in the industry, EDA tools should be very interoperable,” said Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor R&D for advanced packaging technology and manufacturing at Intel. [3]. “I happened to look at a design last week. Just by experience, I said, ‘I don’t see enough density in some of these layers. Copper density is critical for warpage.’ I was very concerned that this might be a technical glitch. I reached out to my mechanical analysis person. I said, ‘Here you go. I think it is one of the other industry formats, but it doesn’t matter. We need to let the design team know that they might have to co-optimize the design, so they don’t get into issues later.’ It took 10 days for the analysis and a response. People looked at the design. They saw it wasn’t complete. It didn’t have some properties. Maybe it wasn’t completely routed. Then I pulled in a design engineer. They finished up with AI. They wrote some scripts, routed it, but then the extraction didn’t happen in a very prominent industry analysis capability. What I got was three pictures. One is yellow. One is red, and who knows what the other color is. And if I am a customer, as a design person, I look at it and don’t know what I need to do to the design. It makes no sense. Then I’ve got to bring 10 PhDs in a room [to fix it].”

Fig. 1: Intel’s Immaneni details the impact of complexity in AI chips. Source: Intel/DAC
Interoperable tools make it easier for customers to bring findings together. “Each of the customers should be able to pick and choose the best in class from each vendor, whether it’s mechanical analysis, design enabling, connectivity checkers, whatever it is. And all these EDA tools should agree to a CAD-neutral format, so the extractions don’t become this complex,” Immaneni noted.
For now, HPC customers are doing the best they can. “We have been living in pain for probably the last five or six years,” said AJ Tufano, distinguished engineer at Broadcom.[2] “We’re getting by, we’re surviving, we’re producing chips, but we can do a lot better.”
In the custom accelerator space, every six months — and in some cases every three months — fundamental architectural changes are happening. “The challenge that we’re faced with is how to match the pace of software, and how to do that while complexity keeps increasing. 3.5D is a large part of that,” Tufano observed.

Fig. 2: Challenges in 3D-IC and heterogeneous design. Source: Broadcom/DAC
There are wins with the challenges. “I will pause and give kudos to the folks creating these tools because it does really impress me that for the scale of the design we have, we can get this thing to run in its entirety at the level of detail that is needed,” said Tufano. “That’s phenomenal. If I look at the number of orders of [magnitude] at any given point in time to do one chip, it’s like a brownout of the lab. The compute resource there is pretty stagnant, so we’re left with a dichotomy of early analysis flows to catch gross issues, which are important, then full-blown IR signoff, which happens much too late. There’s a gap of issues that could potentially be solved in between.”
Others point to similar challenges. [3] “We are surviving right now,” said Venu Sanaka, senior director of engineering at Qualcomm. “The thermal and IR analysis are much more advanced than the other stages of analysis in terms of the multi-physics. The challenges right now are more on the exploration front. Exploration is pretty manual. I can venture out to say, where do you put the bump locations and TSVs (through-silicon vias) and thermal? Those trade-offs aren’t fast enough for our analysis in a normal design cycle. Say it’s one year or so. For this kind of partitioning analysis, we need to start much earlier, maybe three to six months. For that, you don’t have designs ready to run through all the detailed analysis, so you need an early trade-off mechanism.”
Die-to-die PPA optimizations are also tricky. “We wanted to move one block from one die to the other die in a different technology,” said Sanaka. “The power and placement implications of that are all manual right now. We don’t have any quick way of analyzing it, so we floorplan it in 2D, then we put it together and analyze it.”
Multi-chip compounds the challenge. “When I say one chip, I mean when you put in the physical index directory it is related to one chip,” said Sanaka. “Now you have multiple chips trying to come together with different technologies. The data management aspect itself is a little more challenging, and we have a lot of partners within our teams that we need to exchange data with. How do you exchange that data? These are all in the recent stages.”
 Fig. 3:  EDA tool solutions needed by companies designing AI chips. Source: Qualcomm/DAC 
The opportunity to improve tools is large, even if there are pain points right now. “It’s clear that there’s sub-optimality,” Sheng observed. “These chips are phenomenally successful, so it’s okay for now. To fully appreciate the transformation, we’re going from fully manual to automation. We’re going from many single-domain problems to cross-domain problems. In many cases, manual design is experience-driven.”
EDA tools have undoubtedly made incremental improvements, noted Sheng. “But transformational readiness goes through everything.”
Agentic AI as an additional layer on existing tools
EDA vendors have two paths to meet HPC customers’ needs  — augment existing tools or start over. Agentic AI is making both paths possible.
“Three or four years ago, when we saw the technology starting to take off, we had this discussion,” said Vinay Patwardhan, product management group director at Cadence. [3] “When we went to customers, one piece of feedback we received was, ‘We have a hundred 2D designers. We don’t have any 3D designers, so whatever you build, make sure those hundred people can adapt your existing technology.”
Another problem concerned taping out the chip. “We say, ‘It’s a new technology. We just wrote it.’ And the customer would respond, ‘Can you build on something that is trusted so we don’t have to go through this palm tree validation loop again?’ So we made a conscious decision to say that we have our industry-standard tools. The foundries are qualified with extensive certification flows,” Patwardhan explained. “It makes sense to build on that, make it three-dimension aware, use some optimizations to do full 3D or stacking, then see how the industry is moving. When an inflection point comes, we either redevelop the whole flow, or we use some of the new techniques. That’s where we are now with the agentic flow that has come to the top. The exploration capabilities are tremendously improved, and will be tremendously improved because there are a lot of variables.”

Fig. 4: Synopsys’ Sheng and Cadence’s Patwardhan debate the readiness of EDA tools for 3D design at the Design Automation Conference. Source: Semiconductor Engineering [3]
Others agree that agents offer the extra layer needed. “AI is increasingly being used to explore configurations and identify optimal tradeoffs much faster than traditional flows, accelerating design-space exploration, especially for 2.5D and 3D-ICs, where complexity grows significantly,” noted Insaf Meliane, director of product management and marketing, at Arteris. “But AI-generated design decisions must be explainable, traceable, and validated against deterministic EDA engines and established verification methodologies before signoff.”
The latest tools already help with some of the upfront floor-planning analysis for 3D-ICs, and the agentic layer with natural language prompts can be turned on or off to save token use.
“At a very abstract level, we can look at boxes in different colors and with a few clicks, you can change the materials or properties,” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “You can choose to have a very deep via layer, and you can see what the impact would be on your electrical performance. Or you can have a very thin via layer. It’s a choice of, ‘What if?’ This is not a deep optimization problem. This is an architectural problem. The architecture of these designs has some boundary conditions. You can’t just shoot for the moon. Largely, it’s the materials that people are operating in. The size constraint is fixed. The depth constraint, the number of layers you can have, is fixed. For the chiplet die itself, you have a good understanding of whether you are going to do this in 2nm or stay with 6nm, but you may have a little bit of room to negotiate that.”
Electrical performance can already be analyzed in the 3D tool, and IR drop, power integrity, thermal, and other multiphysics will be added soon. “At the floor planning level, not only do you get to see electrical performance, but if you change the package material, what happens to signal performance? What happens to power? What happens to thermal? All of that at a floor-planning level should be available to the architect,” Kamdar noted.
Post-training, continuous learning in agentic AI also offers promise for EDA tools to evolve to the needed complexity.
To enable agentic autonomous research, engineers set up research targets and create a benchmark suite. “You kind of cut your agents loose and say, ‘Here’s what I want you to get better at,’” said Jeff Dyck, vice president of R&D at Siemens EDA. [4] “That’s working extremely well for building better tools. It’s in the self-learning theme, and agents are extremely good at this. Then you say, ‘You guys have to build your own models that are better for this.’ Auto fine-tuning, auto distillation, and the like are strong opportunities in that auto-learning space.”
Agentic AI as the foundation for startup solutions
Many startups aim to disrupt traditional EDA tools with a unique selling proposition that leverages AI and/or agents.
“The platform we built is completely scalable for anything — die level, 3D-IC level, and advanced packaging level,” said Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents. “You can leverage our workflow to solve any kind of problem from chip to system to analog. Then you have to tune the workflow, to make it more advanced, so that your time to results and your cost continue improving, meaning that you can do your advanced packaging in one day instead of taking months. That requires more tuning.”
Fine-tuning of the agentic platform requires strong collaboration with customers. “To achieve this, the customer needs to understand their ontology, their know-how, the way that they are doing certain things,” said Rahim. “The second thing is you need to have both design expertise and domain expertise. Based on that, you can then build some advanced intelligence to tackle those problems. Tuning is building that advanced intelligence, and that advanced intelligence is a brain. You’re actually tuning a brain. We’re not talking about the LLM. We’re talking about a brain sitting in the workflow that is collecting a lot of data, the ontology, and the intelligence of our R&D to solve the customer’s problem and create an algorithm, but that algorithm is much more complex than the traditional algorithm that is capable of taking all this data and working with the LLMs to get to the outcome that you need. That’s what we call the tuning.”
Startup Architect Labs puts proprietary, specialized agents into an end-to-end, full-stack co-design system. “We’re elevating you from an RTL engineer to a human architect,” said Dan Ganousis, head of sales at Architect Labs. “We read the spec and ask, ‘What are you trying to build?’ They say, ‘We’re using a UCIe interface.’ We can go get that. ‘We’re using an Arm core.’ We can go get that and put it in such that the engineer is not writing Verilog to design. He’s writing at the spec level, the architectural level, of what we are trying to accomplish, and then our system takes that, sits on top of all the existing flow, and feeds logic synthesis. We have formal methods that we have customized in our system, so we’re formally verifying as we’re building.”
Another company developed a two-way AI virtual platform, from spec to RTL and from RTL to spec, to enable hardware/software co-design. “With our technology, you give it a spec or model and instead of generating RTL directly, it generates a high-level model, which runs 30´ faster,” said Badru Agarwala, CEO of Rise. “It’s loosely timed. It’s not RTL. Then, using our high-level synthesis tools, you can lower it to RTL. On the other hand, we have other technology that goes from RTL to spec. There, it is the opposite problem. Designers can start verification immediately because these models are timing-dependent. They have all the information, and one advantage of high-level models is that you can explore. If you want to change the memory bandwidth, or you want to change the performance, throughput, timing, 7nm, remove the functionality, all the benefits are available once you have the high-level models to do that.”
Meanwhile, a South Korean startup focuses on a no-code, diagram-first approach to solve power and clock problems in early-stage RTL design. “We make the DFT logic at the RTL design level, so we can shift left the DFT design to the very early stage,” said Jihwan Lee, strategy planning team leader at ITDA. “Our tool is based on a graphical user interface (GUI), so an engineer can just drag and drop the components in our tool and get all the outputs for the synthesis — RTL code and some SDC and UPF for the plug and power synthesis, and DFT tool input file.”
Other companies offer multi-physics simulation tools at extremely high speeds. “There is a crisis in the industry, in my opinion, and the only solution is extremely deep innovation that will give you very high accuracy, but much, much faster,” said Yehea Ismail, co-founder of Suitera, who declined to explain how the high speeds were achieved except that it took seven years.
The shift toward physics-based, AI-enabled tools has proof in the numbers. “A 200-case design sweep that used to take about 16 hours on a legacy thermal workflow now runs in roughly an hour, with setup in under a minute,” said Vinci’s Kabari. “The more telling number, though, is what happens after that. The physics analysis scales near-linearly for runtime inference beyond 10 billion degrees of freedom, because a real system isn’t one component.”
Conclusion
Ultimately, the success of 3D-ICs will depend not only on packaging and process breakthroughs, but also on EDA tools that can keep pace with rapidly changing design requirements. AI tools, machine learning, and agentic systems have value, and there is shared agreement that deterministic physics cannot be left out of the probabilistic AI equation.
From a commercial standpoint, the chip industry consists of EDA, design, and manufacturing. “The technical problem is that these three are still heavily interacting, and so we can see a lot of collaboration,” said Sheng. “If you want to do incremental change [in EDA tools for 3D/HI], each one of these can march forward on its own, but only for a certain amount of time. If you really want non-incremental change, then this has to be done in concert across the three systems. In other words, EDA alone does not optimize what design you can formulate. It’s not that you don’t know what you want. It’s really, can you codify the design and make it programmatic with what you want, and define your boundary conditions in a more disciplined way?”
For now, the physics are not changing. “Light is light, masks are masks,” said Arteris’ Siwinski. “Until we figure out some other way — maybe at some point in the future, there will be some other materials that allow us to make bigger wafers — chiplets are given, 3D packaging is a given, and everything is going to go vertical. Everything needs to be chiplet first, multi-die first, physically-aware first, including package considerations.”
3D is an exciting space. “The fun thing is going to be, will logic dies go the way that memory dies are going?’ Siwinski observed. “Are we really going to start doing 3D logic cubes and rethinking about how packaging is to evolve for that, much more than what’s happening on the memory side? We’ll see.”
— Brendan Heffernan contributed to this report.
